stories.headline: COP31 opens in Türkiye: climate finance falls, electrification push and trade barriers in focus
stories.summary: COP31 has opened in Türkiye with climate finance, electrification and emission curbs dominating the agenda, though several major world leaders stayed away from the leaders' segment. Host Türkiye is championing a voluntary initiative to accelerate electrification of transport, buildings and industry, aiming to raise electricity's share of global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, and a new Electrify Now Finance Coalition was launched with $94 million in catalytic finance to mobilise over $1.2 billion in private investment for grids and clean-energy access in developing countries. UNCTAD reported that only 7% of climate provisions in recent trade deals address barriers to clean-technology access, underlining the technology-transfer gap. Carbon Brief's analysis found that public climate-finance pledges have fallen by more than 70% since earlier rounds, while IFAD warned that El Niño could cause $11 trillion in global income losses and push 49 million people into acute food insecurity by 2027, with Southern Africa and Asia most exposed.
stories.whyItMatters: COP31 crystallises the three persistent fault lines of the climate regime — inadequate finance, weak technology transfer and trade barriers — which directly shape India's NDC delivery, energy transition costs and food-security planning. It is a high-yield source for GS-III questions linking climate equity (CBDR-RC) with trade, agriculture and energy policy.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. The Paris Agreement works through NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the LiFE mission.
static.socioEconomic: Climate finance and technology transfer determine whether developing countries can decarbonise without sacrificing development; the sharp fall in pledged public finance and weak technology-access provisions in trade deals sharpen equity concerns.
static.whyInNews: COP31 in Türkiye opened with climate finance, electrification and emission curbs in focus; Carbon Brief reports public climate-finance pledges down over 70%, and UNCTAD flags that only 7% of climate provisions in recent trade deals address technology barriers.
static.wayForward: Deliver on finance commitments at scale and predictability, operationalise technology transfer and Article 6 carbon-market rules, and embed just-transition safeguards so that mitigation targets do not shift transition costs onto developing economies.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023).
static.mainsAngle: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps; examine equity in the Global Stocktake and just transition.

static.topic: Agriculture, MSP & Food Security
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture & Food Security
static.whatIsIt: Minimum Support Price (MSP) is announced by the government on CACP recommendations for 22 mandated crops. Food security is backed by the National Food Security Act, 2013, and PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana grain distribution.
static.background: The Green Revolution (1960s) made India food-sufficient. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations. PM-KISAN gives ₹6,000/year income support. The three 2020 farm laws were repealed in 2021.
static.geography: IFAD's COP31 warning identifies Southern Africa and Asia as facing severe agricultural risks from El Niño-driven climate shocks.
static.socioEconomic: IFAD warns El Niño could cause $11 trillion in global income losses and push 49 million people into acute food insecurity by 2027, with combined investments in inputs, markets and finance offering the best chance of mitigating losses.
static.whyInNews: An IFAD report released at COP31 links El Niño-driven climate shocks to large global income losses and acute food insecurity, reviving the climate-agriculture-food security linkage in negotiations.
static.wayForward: Combine investments in agricultural inputs, market access and finance; strengthen climate-resilient cropping, early-warning systems and buffer stocks so that climate shocks do not translate into food-security crises.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right; procurement is concentrated in wheat and paddy.
NFSA covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.
static.mainsAngle: Reforming MSP and procurement while raising farmer incomes; water-fertiliser sustainability.

static.topic: Climate Finance & Technology Transfer Architecture
static.syllabusNode: Environment — International Cooperation & Climate Finance
static.whatIsIt: Climate finance flows through the UNFCCC financial mechanism — the Global Environment Facility (GEF) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF, 2010) — alongside multilateral development banks and bilateral channels. Technology transfer is addressed through the Technology Mechanism under the UNFCCC.
static.background: Developed countries committed at Copenhagen (2009) to mobilise $100 billion a year by 2020, a goal that was met late and extended to 2025. The Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). A post-2025 New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance was negotiated at COP29.
static.socioEconomic: Falling public pledges shift the burden towards private and catalytic capital, which may not reach the poorest and most vulnerable countries on affordable terms; trade measures can simultaneously restrict access to clean technology.
static.whyInNews: At COP31, Carbon Brief's analysis shows public climate-finance pledges down over 70%, UNCTAD finds only 7% of climate provisions in recent trade deals address technology barriers, and the Electrify Now Finance Coalition was launched with $94 million in catalytic finance targeting over $1.2 billion in private investment.
static.wayForward: Make finance predictable and grant-based where needed, align trade rules with clean-technology diffusion, and use catalytic public capital to de-risk private investment in grids and clean-energy access in developing countries.
prelimsPointers: The GCF was established in 2010 and the GEF serves as a financial mechanism of the UNFCCC.
The $100 billion-a-year climate finance goal originated in the 2009 Copenhagen Accord and was extended to 2025.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why climate finance and technology transfer remain the weakest links in the global climate regime, and suggest reforms that balance mitigation ambition with developmental equity.

prelims: COP31 is being hosted by Türkiye, which is championing a voluntary electrification initiative targeting a 35% share for electricity in global energy consumption by 2035.
UNCTAD, at COP31, reported that only 7% of climate provisions in recent trade deals address barriers to clean-technology access.
Carbon Brief's analysis found public climate-finance pledges have fallen by more than 70% as countries meet at COP31.

stories.mainsQuestion: Climate finance, technology transfer and trade rules remain the persistent fault lines of global climate negotiations. Examine these issues in the light of COP31 deliberations and evaluate their implications for India's energy transition and developmental priorities.

stories.headline: Bangladesh unrest grows over Sheikh Hasina's planned December return
stories.summary: Bangladesh's political crisis has sharpened around former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's stated plan to return home in December, with arson attacks and crude bomb blasts leaving at least one person dead and buses torched. Dhaka's International Crimes Tribunal, which has tried her in absentia and sentenced her to death over the police crackdown during the July–August 2024 uprising, is central to the standoff: the country's chief prosecutor has said she has no legal option but to submit to the sentence, and has ruled out any passport facility for her. Hasina, who has been in India since she was ousted in August 2024, wants to come back as a political leader and reclaim the Awami League, but faces arrest and execution if she does. The episode has renewed uncertainty over India–Bangladesh ties, with Dhaka seeking her return and New Delhi yet to act on it.
stories.whyItMatters: The case tests how domestic accountability processes and neighbourhood diplomacy interact when a former head of government is the accused, and exposes the limits of extradition law and political asylum in South Asia.

perspectives.take: Frames the story almost entirely through the prosecution's legal assertion — the chief prosecutor's claim that Hasina has no legal route left but to face the death sentence.
Leads with the on-ground violence — one death and torched buses — reading the turmoil as a direct consequence of the return announcement.
Explanatory, Delhi-view framing: sets out Hasina's dilemma between reclaiming the Awami League and facing the ICT's death sentence, listing the hurdles, risks and politics of a return.
Pairs the prosecutor's 'no legal option but execution' line with the day's arson and crude-bomb violence, treating the two as one unfolding crisis.
Headlines the prosecutor's execution remark, foregrounding the legal dead-end and the passport denial for an Indian readership.
Emphasises the administrative bar — the passport ruled out — alongside the prosecutor's statement that execution is unavoidable.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Bilateral Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship between India and Bangladesh covering land and maritime boundaries, river-water sharing, trade and transit, connectivity, security cooperation and people-to-people ties. Bangladesh is India's most important eastern neighbour and a bridge to the Act East Policy and BIMSTEC.
static.background: India's role in the 1971 Liberation War shaped the relationship; the 1972 Indira–Mujib Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Peace (which lapsed in 1997) symbolised the early phase. The 1974 Land Boundary Agreement was operationalised only in 2015 with the exchange of enclaves and adverse possessions. The Ganga Waters Treaty was signed in 1996; the Teesta sharing agreement remains unsigned. An extradition treaty was concluded in 2013 (amended 2016). Relations were at their warmest during Sheikh Hasina's tenures (1996–2001 and 2009–2024), and have been uncertain since her ouster in August 2024.
static.geography: Bangladesh is bounded by India on the west, north and east and by Myanmar's Rakhine region in the southeast, with the Bay of Bengal to the south. India shares its longest land border — roughly 4,096 km — with Bangladesh, and the two countries share 54 common rivers.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is among India's largest trade partners in South Asia, with significant informal trade, a large Bangladeshi diaspora and migrant workforce in India, and deep cross-border family and cultural linkages along the border districts. Political instability in Dhaka transmits quickly to Indian border states and to supply chains.
static.whyInNews: Sheikh Hasina's stated plan to return to Bangladesh in December, the violence it has triggered, and Dhaka's demand for her return have reintroduced a sharp political irritant into India–Bangladesh relations.
static.wayForward: Maintain working channels with whichever government holds office in Dhaka, pursue the pending Teesta agreement through a basin-wide approach, expand connectivity and trade facilitation, and manage border security and migration through institutional mechanisms rather than personality-driven diplomacy.
prelimsPointers: India's land border with Bangladesh is about 4,096 km — the longest India shares with any neighbour.
India and Bangladesh share 54 rivers; the Ganga Waters Treaty of 1996 governs sharing at Farakka.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how political transitions in Bangladesh affect India's neighbourhood policy, and suggest institutional safeguards that can insulate bilateral cooperation from regime change.

static.topic: International Crimes Tribunal and Transitional Justice
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law and Justice; also relevant to Polity (judiciary and accountability)
static.whatIsIt: The International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) is a domestic court of Bangladesh, sitting in Dhaka, that tries genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and other offences under the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973. It is a national tribunal, distinct from UN-ad hoc tribunals and from the International Criminal Court.
static.background: The legal basis is the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act enacted in 1973 to prosecute those accused of atrocities during the 1971 Liberation War; the Act was amended in 2009 and 2013, and the tribunal itself was constituted in 2010. Its verdicts have largely targeted Jamaat-e-Islami and BNP-linked figures. After the student-led July 2024 uprising, cases arising from the police crackdown were brought before it; it has since tried and sentenced Sheikh Hasina in absentia, and she has been convicted in related proceedings.
static.geography: The tribunal sits in Dhaka, Bangladesh; it operates under Bangladeshi law, unlike the ICC at The Hague.
static.socioEconomic: The trials are politically charged: supporters see them as accountability for mass atrocities, while critics describe them as victor's justice in a deeply polarised polity. Verdicts directly affect party politics, street mobilisation and investor confidence.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh's chief prosecutor has publicly stated that Sheikh Hasina has no legal option but to face the death sentence handed down by the ICT, in the context of her announced December return.
static.wayForward: Ensure scrupulous due process and transparent trial standards so verdicts withstand scrutiny, protect the rights of the accused including those tried in absentia, and pair criminal accountability with a broader reconciliation and electoral process to prevent cyclical retribution.
prelimsPointers: The International Crimes Tribunal is a domestic Bangladeshi court, not a UN-established tribunal.
It was constituted in 2010 under the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973, originally aimed at 1971 war-time atrocities.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether domestic tribunals deliver credible transitional justice, using the Bangladeshi experience to weigh accountability against political reconciliation.

static.topic: Extradition, Asylum and International Legal Cooperation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law; India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: Extradition is the formal surrender of an accused or convicted person by one state to another for trial or punishment; asylum is protection extended by a state to a person fleeing persecution. There is no general obligation to extradite in the absence of a treaty, and most treaties contain a political-offence exception and dual-criminality requirements.
static.background: India's law on the subject is the Extradition Act, 1962, and India has extradition arrangements with a large number of countries. The India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty was signed in 2013 and amended in 2016, and it provides that certain grave offences cannot be treated as political offences for the purpose of refusing extradition. Bangladesh has formally sought Sheikh Hasina's return from India; India has not acted on the request.
static.socioEconomic: Extradition disputes carry diplomatic costs: delay or refusal can strain trade, transit and security cooperation, while compliance can create precedent for how a state treats political exiles.
static.whyInNews: With Hasina in India and Dhaka pressing for her return after the ICT death sentence, the extradition question has become the legal core of the current bilateral friction.
static.wayForward: Handle the request through the treaty's own dispute and consultation mechanisms, keep judicial and diplomatic tracks separate, and avoid creating precedents that could be invoked against Indian interests in future cases.
prelimsPointers: India's Extradition Act, 1962 governs extradition requests, which are routed through diplomatic channels.
The India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty was signed in 2013 and amended in 2016.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the tension between treaty-based extradition obligations and the political-offence exception, with reference to recent South Asian cases.

prelims: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's longest-serving Prime Minister (1996–2001 and 2009–2024), resigned and left for India in August 2024 after the student-led July uprising.

The International Crimes Tribunal in Dhaka is a domestic Bangladeshi court set up in 2010 under the International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973; it has tried Hasina in absentia and sentenced her to death.
India shares its longest land border, roughly 4,096 km, with Bangladesh; the two countries share 54 common rivers.
The India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty (2013, amended 2016) is the legal instrument governing Dhaka's request for Hasina's return.
stories.mainsQuestion: The prosecution of a former head of government raises difficult questions for both domestic accountability and neighbourhood diplomacy. Examine the implications of the Sheikh Hasina case for India–Bangladesh relations and for the future of transitional justice in South Asia. (250 words)

stories.headline: Delhi air quality stays 'very poor' as CPCB defends AQI data gaps
stories.summary: Delhi's air quality remained in the 'very poor' category on 11 November 2026, with official AQI readings reported around 299–303 after Deepavali. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) responded to concerns about data gaps at some monitoring stations, an apparent AQI ceiling of 500, and differences between official and private air-quality readings. CPCB explained that PM readings above 1,000 µg/m³ are excluded from the official AQI computation, while stubble burning in neighbouring States continued to contribute to the region's pollution. Sirsa in Haryana recorded the highest AQI at 403, highlighting the wider northern India air-quality challenge.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests understanding of air-quality governance, CPCB's monitoring methodology, and inter-State coordination under CAQM/GRAP; relevant to GS-III environment and GS-II federalism.

perspectives.take: Frames the story around official AQI remaining 'very poor' and CPCB's technical defence for excluding extreme PM readings above 1,000 µg/m³ from the AQI, with a governance-accountability focus.
Emphasises Delhi's post-Deepavali deterioration, AQI at 303, and stubble burning in neighbouring States as a regional contributor; city-centric public-health framing.

Highlights the controversy over the 500 AQI cap, monitoring gaps, and official-versus-private data divergence, while also noting Sirsa's 403 AQI and Delhi's 299 to show a broader Haryana-UP-Delhi pollution belt.

static.topic: Federalism & Centre-State Relations
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States via the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Art. 248).
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201).
static.geography: Delhi-NCR spans Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan; airshed governance requires inter-State coordination.
static.socioEconomic: Air pollution imposes health and economic costs across State boundaries, making cooperative federalism central to mitigation.
static.whyInNews: Delhi-NCR's 'very poor' AQI and CPCB's data-gap defence involve coordination among the Centre, Delhi, Haryana, UP and Punjab.
static.wayForward: Strengthen inter-State airshed management, transparent data-sharing, and institutional mechanisms under CAQM.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless state law reserved for President's assent (Art. 254).
Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Assess cooperative federalism in environmental governance, especially Delhi-NCR airshed management.

static.topic: National Air Quality Index (NAQI) and CPCB
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Pollution & Monitoring
static.whatIsIt: The National Air Quality Index, launched by CPCB in 2015, converts concentrations of eight pollutants—PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and Pb—into a single 0–500 index with six categories from 'Good' to 'Severe'.
static.background: CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and later entrusted with air pollution control under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. AQI was introduced to simplify air-quality communication.
static.geography: Delhi-NCR's landlocked geography, winter inversion, and low wind speeds trap pollutants; regional sources include transport, industry, construction and stubble burning.
static.socioEconomic: Poor air quality affects public health, labour productivity and tourism, with disproportionate impact on children, elderly and outdoor workers.
static.whyInNews: CPCB defended AQI methodology amid concerns over data gaps, the 500 cap, and exclusion of PM readings above 1,000 µg/m³.
static.wayForward: Improve monitor density, real-time transparency, source apportionment, and public communication on AQI limitations.
prelimsPointers: AQI has six categories: Good, Satisfactory, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor, Severe.
CPCB is the national apex pollution control body under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the credibility and limitations of India's AQI system in driving policy and public health responses.

static.topic: Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) and CAQM
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Air Pollution Governance
static.whatIsIt: GRAP is a graded emergency response framework for Delhi-NCR that imposes escalating restrictions on construction, transport, industry and waste burning as AQI worsens; it is now implemented by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM).
static.background: GRAP was introduced in 2016 by the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) and later operationalised under CAQM, established by the CAQM Act, 2021, for the NCR and adjoining areas.
static.geography: Covers Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan districts in the NCR airshed.
static.socioEconomic: Restrictions affect livelihoods, construction activity and mobility, requiring balancing of health emergency measures with economic costs.
static.whyInNews: Delhi's 'very poor' AQI and CPCB's data-gap defence have renewed scrutiny of GRAP triggers and CAQM's regional coordination.
static.wayForward: Link GRAP triggers to transparent, verified AQI data; strengthen regional enforcement and long-term source reduction.
prelimsPointers: CAQM is a statutory body under the CAQM Act, 2021.
GRAP measures are categorised by AQI levels, from 'Poor' to 'Severe+'.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the effectiveness of GRAP and CAQM in reducing Delhi-NCR's winter air pollution.

prelims: Delhi's AQI on 11 Nov 2026 was reported around 299–303, in the 'very poor' category; Sirsa (Haryana) recorded 403, the highest among monitored cities.

stories.headline: US court clears summons route to NSA Doval, ex-RAW chief in Pannun suit
stories.summary: A US court has cleared the way for summonses in a civil suit filed by Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun to be served on India's National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and a former chief of the Research and Analysis Wing, after earlier attempts at service did not succeed. The order permits the plaintiffs to route service through Indian judicial channels rather than through direct service within the United States. India rejected the lawsuit as 'fabricated and malicious', maintaining that the allegations do not reflect official policy. The development adds a legal and procedural dimension to an already sensitive phase in India–US relations, where allegations of transnational targeting of dissidents have been a recurring irritant.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the interface between domestic civil litigation in a foreign jurisdiction, sovereign immunity and diplomatic practice — a recurring UPSC theme under India's bilateral relations and international law. Also relevant to internal security debates on transnational Khalistan activism and the legal limits of countering it.

perspectives.take: Leads on the delivery of summonses to the NSA and a former RAW chief, framing it as a diplomatic discomfort for Delhi rather than a purely legal step.
Emphasises the procedural breakthrough — that after failed attempts, the US court allowed service to be channelled through Indian courts.

static.topic: India–United States Relations: Convergence and Friction
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral Relations (India–US)
static.whatIsIt: The India–US relationship is a broad-based strategic partnership spanning defence, counter-terrorism, trade, technology, energy and people-to-people ties, but it periodically absorbs friction over divergent legal, immigration and human-rights positions.
static.background: Ties were frosty through much of the Cold War and warmed after 1991 economic liberalisation, the 2005 civil nuclear understanding and the 2008 nuclear deal. The relationship was later institutionalised through the 2+2 Ministerial Dialogue, the Quad, foundational defence agreements (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA) and technology initiatives. Disputes over tariffs, visas and legal cases involving Indian officials have recurred alongside the strategic convergence.
static.geography: The two are the world's largest democracies, straddling the Indian and Pacific Oceans; the partnership is central to the Indo-Pacific balance of power.
static.socioEconomic: The Indian diaspora in the US is a major economic and political bridge; two-way trade, services exports and technology collaboration are significant, and US-based diaspora politics can amplify fringe movements such as Khalistan advocacy.
static.whyInNews: A US court has allowed summonses in a civil suit by Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun to be served on India's NSA and a former RAW chief through Indian courts, and India has rejected the suit as fabricated and malicious.
static.wayForward: India should pursue legal remedies through established mutual legal assistance and diplomatic channels while keeping the strategic partnership insulated from litigation-driven friction; sustained consular and diaspora outreach can counter extremist narratives.
keyTerms: iCET (Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology)
prelimsPointers: India–US 2+2 Ministerial Dialogue involves the Foreign and Defence Ministers of both sides.
The Quad comprises India, the US, Japan and Australia.
India was designated a Major Defence Partner of the US in 2016.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how legal and human-rights disputes interact with the strategic logic of the India–US partnership, and suggest institutional mechanisms to prevent such disputes from eroding bilateral trust.

static.topic: Khalistan Movement and Transnational Extremism
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Extremism and the Role of External State and Non-State Actors
static.whatIsIt: The Khalistan movement seeks a separate Sikh homeland and today operates largely as a diaspora-based advocacy and extremist network, with groups such as Sikhs for Justice (SFJ) campaigning abroad for a referendum.
static.background: The movement peaked in India in the 1980s, with militancy in Punjab, the 1984 Operation Blue Star and the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Militancy was largely suppressed by the early 1990s, but diaspora-based outfits revived the demand through referendums, propaganda and, more recently, threats and legal actions abroad.
static.geography: Punjab is the core territorial claim; the movement's operational and funding base is largely in North America, the UK and Australia.
static.socioEconomic: Punjab's prosperity, migration patterns and a large, politically active diaspora sustain the movement's overseas ecosystem, even as domestic support in Punjab remains marginal.
static.whyInNews: The Pannun lawsuit in a US court, now cleared for service of summons on senior Indian officials through Indian courts, is the latest transnational legal front opened by the movement.
static.wayForward: A combination of legal action against designated outfits, calibrated engagement with host governments, counter-radicalisation outreach to diaspora youth and continued development in Punjab is needed to blunt the movement's overseas traction.
prelimsPointers: Sikhs for Justice was banned in India under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act in 2019.
Gurpatwant Singh Pannun was designated an individual terrorist under UAPA in 2020.
UAPA allows the central government to designate an organisation or individual as terrorist under its Fourth Schedule.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the challenges posed by diaspora-based extremist movements to India's internal security and foreign policy, and evaluate the effectiveness of legal bans and diplomatic engagement in countering them.

static.topic: Service of Foreign Summons, Sovereign Immunity and Diplomatic Law
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law and Institutions
static.whatIsIt: Cross-border service of judicial process is the mechanism by which a court in one country formally notifies a defendant in another. It intersects with sovereign immunity, foreign official immunity and diplomatic privileges under international law.
static.background: The Hague Service Convention (1965) standardised service abroad through designated central authorities, and bilateral Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties provide parallel routes; letters rogatory are used where no treaty applies. The US Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, 1976 governs claims against foreign states in US courts, while the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961 codifies diplomatic privileges and immunities. Courts have generally held that serving process on foreign officials raises questions of immunity and comity between states.
static.whyInNews: A US court permitted summonses in a civil suit to be served on India's NSA and a former RAW chief through Indian courts after earlier attempts failed, prompting India to reject the suit as fabricated and malicious.
static.wayForward: India can contest jurisdiction and immunity through counsel in the foreign proceedings while using diplomatic and mutual legal assistance channels to protect serving and former officials; clarity on immunity for non-diplomatic senior officials would strengthen India's legal position in similar future cases.
prelimsPointers: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations was adopted in 1961 and codifies diplomatic privileges and immunities.
Letters rogatory are formal requests from a court in one country to a court in another for judicial assistance.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague in the Netherlands.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse the tension between a foreign court's civil jurisdiction and the sovereign immunity of state officials, and assess how India should balance legal defence with diplomatic management in such cases.

prelims: A US court has allowed summonses in a civil suit filed by Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun to be served through Indian courts.
Those named in the suit include India's National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and a former chief of the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW).
India rejected the lawsuit as 'fabricated and malicious'.
Sikhs for Justice, the outfit associated with Pannun, is banned in India under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
stories.mainsQuestion: The service of foreign judicial summonses on senior Indian officials raises questions of sovereignty, immunity and bilateral trust. Examine the legal and diplomatic implications of such litigation for India–US relations and suggest a principled response framework.

stories.headline: Oil rebounds as Hormuz shipping attacks blunt Iran-US truce hopes
stories.summary: Crude prices rebounded from a two-month low after fresh attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz undercut optimism that Iran and the United States were edging towards a truce. Tehran's top security official said no negotiations with Washington are currently underway, and that the US must first meet seven conditions set out in a June interim agreement before the Strait can reopen and talks resume. Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz within two days, conditional on Washington accepting a package of demands, was said to remain on the table. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said there is 'no need' to attack Iran as diplomatic contacts gather pace. The mixed signals kept oil markets volatile, with traders weighing supply-route risk against the prospect of de-escalation.
stories.whyItMatters: Chokepoint risk in the Strait of Hormuz transmits directly into India's crude import bill, inflation and current account, making Iran–US de-escalation a core energy-security and foreign-policy question. It also tests whether diplomacy or coercion shapes West Asian outcomes, with implications for UNSC-centred multilateralism.

static.topic: Strait of Hormuz — the world's most critical energy chokepoint
static.syllabusNode: Geography — World Geography: Straits, Chokepoints and Maritime Trade Routes
static.whatIsIt: A narrow waterway linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. It is the only sea outlet for the Gulf's oil and gas exporters and therefore the world's most consequential energy chokepoint.
static.background: Tensions over the Strait go back to the Iran–Iraq War of the 1980s, when both sides attacked tankers (the 'Tanker War') and the US reflagged Kuwaiti vessels. The US Fifth Fleet, based in Bahrain, has since underwritten freedom of navigation in the Gulf. The 2015 JCPOA eased pressure; the US exit in 2018 and the return of sanctions revived friction, with periodic seizures and attacks on shipping.
static.geography: Lies between Iran to the north and Oman's Musandam exclave to the south; narrowest width is roughly 39 km, with inbound and outbound shipping lanes separated by a buffer. It connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
static.socioEconomic: Disruption raises freight and insurance costs and oil and LNG prices, inflating import bills for dependent economies such as India. Gulf littoral states' revenues and India's large Gulf diaspora and remittance flows are also exposed.
static.whyInNews: Fresh attacks on shipping in the Strait and Iran's conditional offer to reopen it have whipsawed oil markets and clouded prospects of an Iran–US truce.
static.wayForward: De-escalation and back-channel diplomacy; reaffirmation of freedom of navigation and transit passage under UNCLOS; diversification of supply routes and sources (pipelines, alternate ports); larger strategic reserves and demand-side efficiency.
prelimsPointers: Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman; Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Other key chokepoints: Strait of Malacca, Suez Canal, Panama Canal and the Danish Straits.
UNCLOS provides for 'transit passage' through straits used for international navigation.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how chokepoint geopolitics in West Asia shapes India's energy security, and suggest measures to build resilience against supply-route disruption.

static.topic: India's West Asia policy and energy security
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World: Foreign Policy, Strategic Autonomy and the Extended Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: India's approach to West Asia combines strategic autonomy and multi-alignment — deep energy, trade, diaspora and defence ties with the Gulf states, Israel and Iran, while managing US sanctions and intra-regional rivalries.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954); post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The 'Look West' policy and later 'Link West' deepened Gulf engagement. India partnered with Iran on Chabahar port and joined the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) announced on the sidelines of the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi.
static.geography: West Asia and the Persian Gulf littoral; sea lanes through Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb feed India's western-coast refineries.
static.socioEconomic: India is among the world's largest crude oil importers and a leading recipient of remittances, a large share of which originates in the Gulf. A Hormuz disruption therefore hits the import bill, inflation, the current account and household incomes simultaneously.
static.whyInNews: Attacks on Hormuz shipping and the stalled Iran–US track directly affect India's crude supply, freight costs and diaspora interests.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing and routes; expand strategic petroleum reserves; scale renewables and ethanol/gas blending; use diplomacy to keep sea lanes open; protect diaspora and remittance channels.
prelimsPointers: India's strategic petroleum reserves are located at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
India is the world's third-largest consumer and importer of crude oil.
IMEC was announced on the sidelines of the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India can reconcile its strategic autonomy with its energy dependence on a conflict-prone West Asia.

static.topic: UN & multilateral diplomacy in West Asian crises
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance: UN & Multilateral Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion of the Council; the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: As the US and Iran trade conditions over Hormuz, the crisis again highlights the limits of UNSC action when P5 interests collide, and strengthens the case for Council reform.
static.wayForward: Revive text-based negotiations in the IGN; build coalitions (G4, African Union/Ezulwini Consensus); strengthen regional organisations and preventive diplomacy.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness and contributions; assess the obstacles, including veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

prelims: Iran has linked the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to Washington meeting seven conditions set out in a June interim agreement.

stories.mainsQuestion: Chokepoint disruptions in West Asia are transmitted to India through the crude import bill, freight and insurance costs and diaspora remittances. Examine this transmission in the light of recent developments in the Strait of Hormuz, and suggest a resilience strategy for India.

stories.headline: Nvidia probes alleged spy plot as China chip ties and CEO affair draw scrutiny
stories.summary: Nvidia has opened an internal investigation into allegations that a former executive of Megaspeed spied for China, a claim surfacing alongside a widening federal inquiry into whether the company's advanced chips reached restricted buyers. Reuters, citing records, reports that a Chinese university linked to the People's Liberation Army obtained Nvidia H200 chips despite being on the US blacklist, sharpening questions about export-control enforcement. The controversy has also drawn in CEO Jensen Huang's personal life, with reports of an extramarital affair that commentators say could complicate Nvidia's standing in Washington. Nvidia has issued an internal message to employees, while Huang's personal fortune reportedly fell by $7.4 billion amid the scrutiny. The episode sits at the intersection of US–China technological rivalry, semiconductor supply-chain security and corporate governance at a systemically important firm.
stories.whyItMatters: It shows how export controls, chip supply-chain concentration and leadership conduct intersect — a recurring UPSC theme spanning GS-II (US–China relations), GS-III (semiconductors, indigenisation, corporate governance) and ethics in business.

perspectives.take: Aggregated wire-style report that bundles the China chip-tie scrutiny and the CEO's personal conduct into a single 'deepening scrutiny' narrative.
Business-paper lens across two pieces — an explanatory 'what we know' on the spy-plot probe and a market-focused report on the $7.4 billion hit to Huang's fortune, emphasising investor impact.
Exclusive, records-based investigation focused on enforcement gaps — a PLA-linked Chinese university obtaining H200 chips despite the US blacklist; wire-service, evidence-first framing.
US regional daily carrying the same syndicated Washington-focused analysis; emphasis on domestic political fallout rather than chip-market detail.

static.topic: Semiconductor Supply Chains and the India Semiconductor Mission
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Indigenisation of technology; Economy — Infrastructure: Semiconductors
static.whatIsIt: Semiconductors are materials such as silicon whose conductivity can be precisely controlled; they form the base of integrated circuits used in computing, telecom, defence and automobiles. The value chain spans design (EDA tools and IP cores), fabrication (fabs), assembly-test-mark-pack (ATMP/OSAT), and materials and equipment supply.
static.background: India Semiconductor Mission was launched in December 2021 under MeitY with a ₹76,000 crore outlay, alongside the Semicon India programme and a Production Linked Incentive scheme for large-scale electronics manufacturing. Commercial fab and ATMP/OSAT projects have since been approved, including in Gujarat. Globally, the US CHIPS and Science Act (2022) and the EU Chips Act subsidise domestic capacity, while Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and the Netherlands dominate key stages.
static.geography: Indian clusters: Dholera and Sanand (Gujarat), Jagiroad (Assam), Noida (Uttar Pradesh). Global hubs: Taiwan (foundry), South Korea and Japan (memory and materials), Netherlands (lithography equipment), United States (design and equipment).
static.socioEconomic: Chip shortages ripple into automobiles, consumer electronics and defence procurement; self-reliance is tied to jobs, exports, and strategic autonomy in a concentrated global market.
static.whyInNews: Nvidia's China-linked export-control troubles and the alleged spy plot have renewed attention on chip supply-chain security, export controls and the risks of depending on a handful of firms and geographies.
static.wayForward: Deepen the domestic design ecosystem, secure critical minerals and equipment access, build a talent pipeline, and pursue trusted-supply partnerships with like-minded economies.
prelimsPointers: India Semiconductor Mission (2021) is implemented by MeitY with a ₹76,000 crore outlay.
Nvidia is a fabless company — it designs GPUs and outsources fabrication, mainly to TSMC in Taiwan.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) administers the Entity List under the Export Administration Regulations.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how export controls and supply-chain concentration shape India's semiconductor self-reliance strategy.

static.topic: US–China Technological Rivalry and Export Controls
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; GS-III — Security
static.whatIsIt: US export controls restrict the transfer of advanced semiconductors, chipmaking equipment and related technology to China on national-security grounds, using instruments such as the Entity List and the Foreign Direct Product Rule.
static.background: The US tightened controls progressively from 2018 (ZTE and Huawei listings) and issued sweeping advanced-computing and chipmaking rules in October 2022, further tightened in 2023 and 2024. Nvidia designed downgraded China-specific chips to stay compliant. China retaliated with export curbs on gallium, germanium and graphite, materials critical to chipmaking.
static.geography: United States (design, equipment), Taiwan (foundry), Netherlands (lithography), South Korea and Japan (memory, materials), China (assembly, rare earths and critical materials).
static.socioEconomic: Controls raise compliance costs, fragment supply chains, accelerate Chinese import substitution, and can affect global chip prices and availability.
static.whyInNews: Reports that a PLA-linked Chinese university obtained Nvidia H200 chips despite the US blacklist, alongside federal probes into export-control compliance and possible national-security breaches.
static.wayForward: Multilateral coordination with allies, targeted rather than blanket controls, and hedging through domestic capacity building and diversified sourcing.
prelimsPointers: The Entity List is maintained by the US Bureau of Industry and Security, under the Department of Commerce.
The US CHIPS and Science Act (2022) subsidises domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research.
China has imposed export controls on gallium and germanium, key chip-making materials.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how US–China technological rivalry affects India's strategic autonomy and its supply-chain choices.

static.topic: Corporate Governance, Key-Man Risk and Disclosure
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Corporate governance; GS-IV — Ethics in business and corporate conduct
static.whatIsIt: Corporate governance is the system by which companies are directed and controlled — covering board accountability, timely disclosure, and protection of shareholder interests. Key-man risk is the risk that a firm's value and stability depend disproportionately on one individual.
static.background: India's framework rests on the Companies Act, 2013, the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. The Kotak Committee (2017) recommended governance reforms including greater board independence. Globally, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) followed the Enron collapse.
static.socioEconomic: Governance failures erode investor confidence, raise the cost of capital, and can invite regulatory action against systemically important firms.
static.whyInNews: Nvidia's internal probe and the reported $7.4 billion hit to Jensen Huang's fortune have raised questions about leadership conduct, disclosure practices and key-man risk at a globally significant company.
static.wayForward: Strengthen independent boards, whistleblower mechanisms and timely material disclosure, while separating personal-conduct issues from corporate disclosures that affect investors.
prelimsPointers: SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 govern listing obligations and disclosure requirements for listed entities in India.
The Kotak Committee (2017) recommended reforms including greater board independence and stronger audit committee roles.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss why key-man risk and leadership conduct matter for corporate governance in globally significant firms.

prelims: Nvidia is a fabless chip designer; its advanced AI chips are fabricated mainly by TSMC in Taiwan.
US export controls are administered by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) under the Department of Commerce through the Export Administration Regulations and the Entity List.
India Semiconductor Mission (2021), under MeitY, has a ₹76,000 crore outlay to build fabs and ATMP/OSAT capacity.

stories.mainsQuestion: The weaponisation of semiconductor export controls is reshaping global supply chains and corporate behaviour. Examine the implications for India's semiconductor self-reliance mission and its strategic autonomy.

stories.headline: US House Republicans block Hegseth impeachment bid; Democrats may revive it in January
stories.summary: The US House of Representatives voted 211-204 on 10 November 2026 to refer an impeachment resolution against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, a procedural step by the Republican majority that halts the immediate impeachment drive without extinguishing it. President Donald Trump welcomed the outcome, praising Hegseth as a 'Great American Patriot' and declaring that the effort had 'miserably FAILED!'. The resolution had been pushed by Democrats amid sustained criticism of Hegseth's conduct at the Pentagon, and the party — fresh from a midterm 'blue wave' — retains the option of reviving it once it takes control of Congress in January. The likely incoming chair of the House oversight committee, Democrat Robert Garcia, has signalled aggressive scrutiny of the administration, indicating that the vote is the opening rather than the end of the confrontation.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live case study of the US separation of powers, the essentially political character of impeachment, and how midterm verdicts reshape legislative oversight of defence and foreign policy. For India, changes in the US defence leadership and congressional mood bear directly on defence-industrial cooperation, technology transfer and alliance commitments.

perspectives.take: Frames the vote as a temporary reprieve for Hegseth — Trump's praise is reported alongside the caveat that Democrats can try again next year; neutral wire-style framing.

Emphasises the 211-204 procedural referral to the Judiciary Committee and the January revival window; sober, India-facing international coverage.

static.topic: Legislative Oversight and Impeachment as a Constitutional Check
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Impeachment is the constitutional mechanism by which a legislature removes a high executive or judicial office-holder for serious misconduct; it is the strongest, and most political, instrument of legislative oversight over the executive.
static.background: In India, the President can be impeached only for violation of the Constitution under Article 61, after a 14-day notice and a special majority in each House; Supreme Court and High Court judges are removed under Articles 124(4) and 218 through a similar special-majority process. In the United States, the House of Representatives has the sole power of impeachment and the Senate conducts the trial, where conviction requires a two-thirds majority. The supplied knowledge card notes that Parliament (Article 79) comprises the President and the two Houses, and that departmentally related standing committees are the routine instrument of legislative scrutiny.
static.whyInNews: The US House voted 211-204 to refer an impeachment resolution against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, halting the immediate drive while leaving it open to revival in January.
static.wayForward: Strengthen committee-based scrutiny and protected debate time so that oversight does not collapse into pure adversarialism; in India, this means greater referral of Bills to standing committees and reduced disruption of sittings.
prelimsPointers: OhmA no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
OhmA Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Compare the impeachment and removal mechanisms for constitutional office-holders in India and the US, and assess whether legislative oversight of the executive has weakened in recent decades.

static.topic: Judicial Review and Checks and Balances
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: Judicial review is the power of courts to test the constitutionality of legislative and executive action; along with legislative oversight it forms the second great check in a separation-of-powers system.
static.background: The Indian collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 and 226 provide writ jurisdiction to the Supreme Court and High Courts respectively.
static.whyInNews: The US impeachment referral shows the political branches settling a dispute internally for now; courts remain the other check, while the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress has promised intensified oversight of the administration.
static.wayForward: Balance judicial independence with accountability by addressing vacancies and pendency, so that judicial review remains a credible check rather than a delayed one.
prelimsPointers: OhmOriginal jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes lies with the Supreme Court under Article 131.
OhmThe advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is exercised under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how judicial review and legislative oversight together sustain constitutional accountability, and what happens when one of the two checks is politically blunted.

prelims: The US House voted 211-204 to refer the impeachment resolution against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively halting the immediate impeachment attempt.

stories.mainsQuestion: Impeachment is often described as a political rather than a purely legal process. stories.headline: Six coaches of Sairang–Kolkata Express derail in Assam; casualty reports differ
stories.summary: Six coaches of the Sairang–Kolkata Express went off the tracks at Digaru railway station in Assam on the morning of 11 November 2026, with Mint placing the derailment at about 6:54 a.m. Telegraph India reported that the engine as well as six coaches left the rails, indicating the locomotive was also affected. Accounts of casualties diverge sharply: The Hindu's live coverage said no injuries had been reported so far, while Mint and Telegraph India both reported several passengers injured. Rescue and relief operations were underway at the site, and railway authorities arranged alternate trains to help stranded passengers reach their destinations. The incident once again turns attention to derailment safety on the Indian Railways network.
stories.whyItMatters: Railway derailments are the most frequent category of serious rail accidents in India and directly test the country's rail-safety architecture, disaster-response systems and infrastructure-investment priorities — a recurring GS-III theme.

static.topic: Railway Safety and Accident Investigation in India
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure — Railways: safety, regulation and modernisation
static.whatIsIt: Indian Railways is a departmental undertaking under the Ministry of Railways, operating under the Railways Act, 1989. Serious train accidents are mandatorily inquired into by the Commissioner of Railway Safety (CRS), a statutory authority placed under the Ministry of Civil Aviation rather than the Railways itself, so that the inquiry is institutionally independent of the operator.
static.background: The Railway Safety Review (Kakodkar) Committee, 2012, examined the causes of accidents and recommended a dedicated non-lapsable safety fund and a statutory Railway Safety Authority. The Rashtriya Rail Sanraksha Kosh (RRSK) was created in 2017-18 with a corpus of about ₹1 lakh crore to be used over five years for safety-related works such as track renewal, bridge rehabilitation and signalling upgrades. The Bibek Debroy Committee (2015) separately examined railway restructuring. Derailments have historically accounted for the largest share of serious rail accidents, with causes ranging from track defects and rolling-stock issues to human error and sabotage.
static.geography: The derailment occurred at Digaru railway station in Assam, on the rail corridor linking the Brahmaputra valley with Sairang in Mizoram, near Aizawl. The Northeast Frontier Railway zone covers this region, where terrain, monsoon damage and ageing infrastructure pose particular safety challenges.
static.socioEconomic: Rail accidents cause loss of life and injury, disrupt passenger and freight movement, damage public confidence in the network, and impose compensation and operational costs. For the Northeast, rail connectivity is a strategic as well as an economic lifeline, so disruptions carry outsized regional impact.
static.whyInNews: Six coaches of the Sairang–Kolkata Express derailed at Digaru in Assam on 11 November 2026, with the engine also reported off the tracks and conflicting reports on passenger injuries.
static.wayForward: Accelerate track renewal and bridge rehabilitation using RRSK funds, fast-track deployment of the indigenously developed Kavach anti-collision system, strengthen human-factor management (crew fatigue, training, counselling), and consider an empowered statutory safety authority as recommended by the Kakodkar Committee. Timely publication of CRS inquiry findings would improve accountability.
prelimsPointers: The Commissioner of Railway Safety, who holds statutory inquiries into serious rail accidents, functions under the Ministry of Civil Aviation — not the Ministry of Railways.
The Rashtriya Rail Sanraksha Kosh was set up in 2017-18 with a corpus of about ₹1 lakh crore for a five-year period for safety-related works.
Kavach is an indigenously developed anti-collision system (Train Collision Avoidance System) developed by RDSO for the Indian Railways.
static.mainsAngle: Derailments remain the most frequent form of serious railway accident in India. Examine the structural and operational causes and evaluate whether India's rail-safety architecture — statutory inquiries, dedicated safety funding and technological interventions — is adequate.

static.topic: Disaster Management and Emergency Response to Rail Accidents
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — institutional framework and response mechanisms
static.whatIsIt: India's disaster management framework rests on the Disaster Management Act, 2005, which created the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) chaired by the Prime Minister, State Disaster Management Authorities (SDMAs) chaired by Chief Ministers, and District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs). The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) provides specialised response capability, while the National Institute of Disaster Management handles capacity building.
static.background: The DM Act, 2005, was enacted after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and marked a shift from a relief-centric to a preparedness-and-mitigation-centric approach. Rail accidents are typically handled through the district administration, state police, railway medical and rescue teams, with NDRF assistance for major incidents. The National Disaster Management Plan (2016, revised 2019) covers transport accidents among its hazard-specific provisions.
static.geography: Digaru lies in Assam's Kamrup region, where road and rail access to the accident site, monsoon conditions and proximity to Guwahati determine how quickly rescue and medical support can be mobilised.
static.socioEconomic: Rapid, well-coordinated rescue reduces fatalities and long-term disability, while compensation, ex-gratia relief and hospital care shape the post-accident burden on affected families and the state.
static.whyInNews: Rescue and relief operations were underway after the derailment, with railway authorities arranging alternate trains for stranded passengers.
static.wayForward: Strengthen district-level rail accident response drills, integrate railway control rooms with SDMA/DDMA emergency operations centres, and ensure pre-positioned medical and heavy-lift equipment along high-density corridors.
prelimsPointers: The Disaster Management Act, 2005, established NDMA, SDMAs and DDMAs; the Prime Minister chairs NDMA.
NDRF is a specialised response force under the DM Act framework, deployed for major accidents and disasters.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India's disaster management institutions interface with railway accident response, and suggest measures to reduce response time and improve coordination in rail emergencies.

prelims: Six coaches of the Sairang–Kolkata Express derailed at Digaru railway station in Assam on 11 November 2026, with the engine also reported off the tracks.

stories.mainsQuestion: Derailments continue to be the most frequent category of serious railway accidents in India. Examine the causes of such accidents and evaluate the adequacy of India's rail-safety architecture, including statutory inquiry mechanisms, dedicated safety funding and technological interventions such as Kavach.

stories.headline: Hijack threat note found on Air India Kolkata-Mumbai flight; aircraft moved to isolation bay
stories.summary: A hijack threat note was found on board an Air India flight scheduled to operate from Kolkata to Mumbai, prompting action before the aircraft took off. Passengers who had already boarded were deboarded, and the aircraft was moved to an isolation bay at Kolkata airport — a remote parking position used during security alerts. Standard airport security protocol, including threat assessment and a search of the aircraft, was set in motion. Telegraph India attributed the initial report to a television channel, indicating that some details are yet to be independently confirmed. The reports available do not establish the origin or credibility of the note, and no injuries were reported.
stories.whyItMatters: Aviation security and the handling of hijack or bomb threats sit at the intersection of internal security, transport infrastructure and India's international obligations under ICAO-linked conventions — a recurring theme in GS-III internal security and GS-II international institutions questions.

perspectives.take: Frames the incident operationally as a 'what we know' explainer, foregrounding the movement of the aircraft to an isolation bay on Wednesday morning with limited attribution on the note itself.
Emphasises the passenger-handling sequence — all boarded passengers deboarded before the aircraft was taken to the isolation bay; sober, procedural, national-daily framing.
Presents it as a pre-take-off alert and explicitly credits a television report, signalling hedged sourcing; a Kolkata-based regional lens on a local airport event.

static.topic: Civil aviation security architecture in India
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Security challenges and their management; various security forces and agencies and their mandate
static.whatIsIt: The layered system that protects Indian airports and aircraft: the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) as apex regulator, the CISF for airport security, airline and airport-operator AVSEC staff, and specialised response arrangements for bomb and hijack threats.
static.background: Civil aviation security in India is governed by the Aircraft Act, 1934 and the Aircraft Rules, 1937, with BCAS functioning as the apex regulatory authority under the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016 replaced the 1982 law, widened the definition of hijacking and provides for life imprisonment, or death where the offence results in death. The National Security Guard is the designated national counter-hijack force. At airports, a Bomb Threat Assessment Committee evaluates threats and decides the response, which can include moving an aircraft to an isolation bay.
static.socioEconomic: Security incidents and hoax threats impose direct costs on airlines — diversions, delays, aircraft searches and idle capacity — and erode passenger confidence in a sector where India is among the world's fastest-growing aviation markets.
static.whyInNews: A hijack threat note was found on board an Air India Kolkata-Mumbai flight before take-off, leading to deboarding of passengers and movement of the aircraft to an isolation bay at Kolkata airport.
static.wayForward: Standardise and audit threat-response drills across airports, strengthen intelligence-sharing among BCAS, CISF and state police, tighten pre-flight screening and access controls for catering and cleaning staff, and prosecute hoax threats swiftly to deter copycat incidents.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's airport security regime is equipped to handle the rising incidence of bomb and hijack threats, and suggest institutional and technological reforms.

static.topic: International legal framework against unlawful interference with civil aviation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Important international institutions, agencies and fora: their structure and mandate
static.whatIsIt: A set of international conventions, coordinated by ICAO, that criminalise hijacking and other acts of unlawful interference with civil aviation and oblige states to prosecute or extradite offenders.
static.background: The Chicago Convention, 1944 established the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), a UN specialised agency headquartered in Montreal, which sets global aviation security standards through Annex 17 to the Convention. The Tokyo Convention, 1963 addresses offences committed on board aircraft; the Hague Convention, 1970 deals with the unlawful seizure of aircraft; and the Montreal Convention, 1971 addresses unlawful acts against the safety of civil aviation. India is a party to these instruments and has given effect to them through the Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016.
static.whyInNews: The hijack threat note found on an Air India flight at Kolkata highlights the obligations India carries under these conventions and under ICAO security standards.
static.wayForward: Deepen cooperation through ICAO audits and information-sharing, update domestic law to cover emerging threats such as cyber interference with aviation systems, and pursue multilateral arrangements on passenger data exchange.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how international conventions and ICAO standards shape India's domestic aviation security law, and assess the gaps in enforcement.

static.topic: UN system, specialised agencies and multilateral reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global governance; United Nations and its reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN, founded in 1945, has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members. Specialised agencies such as ICAO, WHO and ILO work under the UN umbrella on sectoral mandates.
static.background: India is a founding member of the UN and among the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for expansion of the Security Council, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) process on reform remains inconclusive. India's aviation security obligations flow from ICAO, a UN specialised agency.
static.whyInNews: The incident draws attention to the UN-linked technical agencies, such as ICAO, that set the standards India's aviation security regime implements.
static.wayForward: Continue pressing for UNSC reform through the G4 and the IGN process while deepening engagement with UN specialised agencies to shape global technical standards.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness, population and peacekeeping contributions; assess the obstacles, including veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

stories.mainsQuestion: Hijack and bomb threats disrupt civil aviation operations and impose heavy costs on carriers and passengers. Examine the adequacy of India's aviation security architecture and legal framework for handling such threats, and suggest reforms.

stories.headline: Telangana widens probe into illegal oocyte harvesting; 27 ART centres inspected
stories.summary: The Telangana government has ordered a statewide investigation into an alleged illegal human egg (oocyte) harvesting and sale racket, with health authorities inspecting 27 assisted reproductive technology (ART) centres and issuing notices to seven hospitals. The probe is not limited to clinics: it also covers the women identified in the case, doctors, IVF centres and intermediaries suspected of facilitating the collection and movement of oocytes. The racket points to a shadow market in reproductive tissue that operates around, and sometimes through, registered fertility facilities. It has renewed scrutiny of how India's fertility industry is licensed, monitored and penalised under the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021, and of the economic coercion that pushes poor women into donating or selling their eggs.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the enforcement capacity of India's ART regulatory architecture and raises bioethics, health-governance and women's-rights questions — a recurring GS-II theme with prelims value on the ART and Surrogacy Acts.

perspectives.take: Frames the development primarily as a governance response — a statewide probe ordered into an illegal human egg harvesting racket, foregrounding the scale of the racket and the state's accountability.
Frames it as an enforcement story with granular detail — 27 ART centres inspected, notices to seven hospitals, and a widening net that includes women, doctors, IVF centres and intermediaries.

static.topic: Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Health; statutory regulation of medical technology and bioethics
static.whatIsIt: A central law that regulates the practice of assisted reproductive technology in India — it makes registration of ART clinics and ART banks mandatory, sets standards for gamete and embryo handling, and creates the National ART and Surrogacy Board along with State ART and Surrogacy Boards. It is the principal legal instrument governing oocyte donation, storage and use.
static.background: India's fertility sector was earlier governed only by the non-statutory ICMR National Guidelines for Accreditation, Supervision and Regulation of ART Clinics (2005), which lacked enforceable penalties. Multiple draft ART Bills were circulated from around 2010 onwards, and the ART (Regulation) Act was finally enacted in 2021 alongside the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021. Rules under the ART Act were subsequently notified, operationalising registration and compliance requirements for clinics and banks.
static.geography: Telangana, with Hyderabad as a major private fertility-treatment hub, illustrates how ART demand concentrates in metropolitan centres and draws donors from surrounding and poorer districts.
static.socioEconomic: Oocyte donation is often mediated by intermediaries and shaped by debt, low incomes and limited livelihood options, raising concerns of informed consent, coercion and commodification of women's bodies.
static.whyInNews: A statewide probe in Telangana into an alleged illegal oocyte collection and sale racket has led to inspections of 27 ART centres and notices to seven hospitals, with doctors, IVF centres and intermediaries under scrutiny.
static.wayForward: Strengthen registration audits and surprise inspections, build a traceable digital registry of gamete donors and cycles, enforce informed-consent and counselling protocols, and impose proportionate penalties on unregistered or exploitative operators while protecting genuine donors.
prelimsPointers: The ART (Regulation) Act, 2021 makes registration of ART clinics and banks mandatory and provides for National and State ART and Surrogacy Boards.
The companion Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 prohibits commercial surrogacy and permits only altruistic surrogacy under specified conditions.
The earlier ICMR National Guidelines (2005) on ART clinics were advisory in nature, not statutory.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's ART regulatory framework adequately protects oocyte donors from exploitation, and suggest institutional reforms to make the fertility sector transparent and accountable.

static.topic: Federalism and health regulation: who polices the fertility industry?
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution; distribution of legislative powers
static.whatIsIt: Public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries are State List subjects, while the Union legislates on matters of national standards such as medical technology and drugs. The result is a shared enforcement space: a central statute like the ART Act is implemented through State-level boards and health machinery.
static.background: The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution divides powers between the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, with residuary powers resting with the Union. Commissions such as Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) examined Centre-State balance. In practice, centrally enacted regulatory statutes in health depend heavily on State inspection and licensing capacity.
static.socioEconomic: Weak State inspection capacity in a high-demand, high-margin private health sector creates regulatory gaps that informal intermediaries exploit.
static.whyInNews: The Telangana government's statewide probe and the inspection of ART centres show State health administration acting as the enforcement arm for a centrally legislated regulatory regime.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise joint Centre-State inspection protocols, share compliance data between the National and State Boards, and build dedicated State-level ART monitoring cells with public reporting.
prelimsPointers: Public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries are State List subjects under the Seventh Schedule.
On Concurrent List subjects, Union law prevails in case of repugnancy unless the State law has been reserved for and given the President's assent (Article 254).
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the division of legislative and administrative competence between the Union and States affects the enforcement of health-sector regulation in India.

static.topic: Welfare, vulnerability and the commodification of women's reproductive labour
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare & Rights; health equity and protection of vulnerable groups
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare architecture combines rights-based legislation with direct benefit transfer and a Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile delivery backbone. Where welfare reach is thin, informal markets — including in reproductive services — can become a survival strategy for poor households.
static.background: Rights-based laws such as MGNREGA (2005), the RTE Act (2009) and the NFSA (2013) expanded entitlements, while Ayushman Bharat (2018) added a health-insurance arm and Health and Wellness Centres. Articles 15 and 16, along with Indra Sawhney (1992), frame the constitutional commitment to substantive equality.
static.socioEconomic: Economic distress, indebtedness and limited employment options can make paid oocyte donation appear as a rational choice, blurring the line between consent and coercion and raising questions of distributive justice.
static.whyInNews: The Telangana racket investigation has drawn attention to the women at the centre of the case, highlighting how economic vulnerability can be converted into exploitative reproductive labour.
static.wayForward: Pair strict enforcement with donor-protection measures — mandatory counselling, compensation norms, post-donation health follow-up, and stronger social security so that donation is never a distress sale.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Ayushman Bharat (2018) has a health-insurance arm (PM-JAY) and a network of Health and Wellness Centres.
static.mainsAngle: Illegal oocyte harvesting is as much a welfare failure as a regulatory one. Critically examine this statement with reference to the protection of economically vulnerable women.

prelims: The ART (Regulation) Act, 2021 regulates ART clinics and banks, mandates their registration, and establishes the National ART and Surrogacy Board with corresponding State Boards.
The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 bans commercial surrogacy and allows only altruistic surrogacy under prescribed conditions.
The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994 prohibits prenatal sex determination and sex-selective practices in diagnostic facilities.
Public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries fall in the State List, making State health departments the primary enforcement machinery for health regulation.
stories.mainsQuestion: The recent crackdown on an illegal oocyte harvesting racket exposes both regulatory and welfare failures in India's fertility sector. Examine the regulatory framework governing assisted reproductive technology in India and suggest measures to protect vulnerable donors without restricting legitimate access to fertility treatment.

stories.headline: Supreme Court disposes reference on states' power to levy sales tax surcharge
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has disposed of a reference concerning whether states can impose a surcharge on sales tax. The question turned on the scope of state legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule and the constitutional treatment of a surcharge as either a separate tax or an increment to an existing state tax. The disposal is expected to bring clarity to state revenue powers and the limits of fiscal federalism. It also has implications for Centre-State tax relations and the interpretation of taxing entries in the Constitution.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests understanding of fiscal federalism, Seventh Schedule taxation entries, and the Supreme Court's role in resolving constitutional questions on state taxing powers. Useful for GS-II polity and GS-III economy questions on devolution and GST-era taxation.

perspectives.take: Reports the Court's disposal of the reference as a constitutional resolution on state taxing power; legal-reporting focus, court-centric and neutral.

static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Article 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201).
static.socioEconomic: State taxation powers affect fiscal autonomy, revenue mobilisation and inter-state tax competition.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court disposed of a reference on whether states can impose a surcharge on sales tax, raising questions of state legislative competence and fiscal federalism.
static.wayForward: Constitutional clarity on state taxing entries, coupled with cooperative federalism through the GST Council and Finance Commission, can reduce Centre-State tax disputes.
